↳ Signal strength is conditioned on a doji appearing as a component of another reversal pattern: a doji as the middle bar of a three-candlestick evening star (evening doji star) makes the pattern more ominous; a doji as the second candle in a harami (harami cross) increases the pattern's implications.
Commentary Bearish Deliberation As illustrated in Figure 3-113, the Bearish Deliberation pattern is also a derivative of the Three White Soldiers pattern. The first two long white candlesticks make a new high and are followed by a small white candlestick or a star. This pattern is also called a Stalled pattern in some literature. It is best if the last day gaps above the second day. Being a small body, this shows the indecision necessary to arrest the upmove. This indecision is the time of deliberation. A further confirmation could easily turn this pattern into an Evening Star pattern.

When price action is primarily one-sided, the real bodies in a directional move will generally be average-sized or longer and their color will reflect the trend's direction. When the bulls are dominating while a stock is rallying, for instance, the candlesticks will be primarily white. Conversely, when the bears are dominating during a decline, the candles will be primarily black. Thus, when one or more diminishing bodies appear after a price advance or decline, it indicates that the dominating party may be losing control of the move. In fact, a spinning top is a component of several reversal patterns.

A doji can stand on its own merit, but it also is a component of other candlestick patterns. If a doji appears as part of another formation, it strengthens the signal. Some examples include the following: If the middle bar of a three-candlestick evening star is a doji, the pattern is more ominous. In that case, it would be referred to as an evening doji star. If a doji appears as the second candle in a harami, it will increase that pattern's implications and would be referred to as a harami cross.

Bullish harami: This bullish counterpart to the bearish harami forms after a price decline. It is formed from two candlestick lines. The first candle’s long black real body is followed by a noticeably smaller real body, either black or white, that resides within the prior candle’s longer body. ... Morning star: This bullish counterpart to the evening star forms after a price decline. It is comprised of three candlestick lines. The first candle has a long black real body. The second candle gaps down open and forms a small real body, either black or white, or a doji, creating the star portion of the pattern. The third candle has a white real body that intrudes deeply into the first candle’s long bearish real body. The deeper the intrusion, the more likely a reversal will follow, especially if the third candle is accompanied by heavy volume.

Figure 4-54 Commentary Bullish Mat Hold The bullish Mat Hold pattern is a modified version of the Rising Three Methods. The first three days start out like the Upside Gap Two Crows, with the exception that the second black body (third day) dips into the body of the first long white day (Figure 4-53). This is followed by another small black body that closes even lower, but still within the range of the first white body. The fifth day sees a large gap opening, with a strong rise to a close above the high of the highest of the three black days. This suggests that the trend will continue upward and that new positions can be taken here. The bullish Mat Hold Pattern shows greater strength as a continuation signal than the Rising Three Methods. The reaction days are basically higher than the ones in the Rising Three Methods. In other words, the bullish Mat Hold does not take quite the rest, or break from trend, that the Rising Three methods does. Rules of Recognition Bearish Deliberation 1. The first and second day have long white bodies. 2. The third day opens near the second day's close. 3. The third day is a Spinning Top and most probably a star. Bullish Deliberation 1. The first day of the pattern is a long black day that occurs in a downtrend. 2. The second day is also a long black day. 3. The third day is a Star or relatively small black day that may gap away from the prior day's black real body. Scenarios and Psychology behind the Pattern Bullish Deliberation ... First, the high-low range of the third day is less than that of the second day. Specifically, it is less than 75% of the second day's high-low range. Second, the body range of the third day is less than the body range of the second day. The program requires that it be less than 50% of the second day's body range. Third and last, even though the black real body of the third day may gap away from the black real body of the second day, the gap is less than 20% of the second day's high-low range.

Chapter Four Commentary The Three Methods (Chapter 5) include the bullish Rising Three Methods and the bearish Falling Three Methods. Both are continuation patterns that represent breaks in the trend of prices without causing a reversal. They are days of rest in the market action and can be used to add to positions, if already in the market. Rising Three Method A long white candlestick is formed in an uptrend (Figure 4-48). After this long day, a group of small-bodied candlesticks occur, which shows some resistance to the previous trend. These reaction days are generally black, but most importantly, their bodies all fall within the high-low range of the first long white day. Remember that the highlow range includes the shadows. The final candlestick (normally the fifth day) opens above the close of the previous reaction day and then closes at a new high. Falling Three Methods The Falling Three Methods pattern is the bearish counterpart of the Rising Three Methods pattern. A downtrend is underway, when it is further perpetuated with a long black candlestick (Figure 4-49). The next thr

rested, even though the price action surely brings out the bears. The next couple of days cause some concern that the upward move may be in jeopardy. These days open about where the market closed on the previous day and then close slightly lower. Even by the third such day, the market is still higher than the open of the first day (a long white day). An attitude that a reversal has failed develops and prices rise again to close at a new closing high. This fully supports the bulls' case that this was just a pause in a strong upward trend. Bearish Mat Hold Days two, three, and four are the break in the trend, and you will notice that they never close above the open of the first day. So, by the end of day four, traders are beginning to think that any reversal of the downtrend has failed. When the fifth day closes below the open of the second day, the bears know that the prior three days were just a pause in a strong downward trend. stair A push to a new extreme in a trending trading range trend or a broad channel trend where there is a series of three or more trending swings that resembles a sloping trading range and is roughly contained in a channel. After the breakout, there is a breakout pullback that retraces at least slightly into the prior trading range, which is not a requirement of other trending trading ranges. Two-way trading is taking place but one side is in slightly more control, accounting for the slope.

When an inside bar occurs after a big trend bar that breaks out of a trading range, it could be simply a pause by the trend traders, but it could also be a loss of conviction that will lead to a reversal (failed breakout). A reversal is more likely when the small bar is an inside bar and it is a trend bar in the opposite direction of the large breakout bar. A with-trend inside bar increases the chances that the breakout move will continue. Small inside bars after breakout trend bars are somewhat emotional for traders because they will consider entering in either direction on a stop. For example, if there is a bull breakout during a down day, the trader will often place an order to buy at one tick above the high of the inside bar and a second order to sell at one tick below its low. Once one order is filled, the other order becomes the protective stop.

All channels eventually end in a breakout, which can be violent or have very little momentum. Trend channels usually last much longer than what most traders suspect and they often trap traders into prematurely taking reversal trades. Most channels usually have at least three legs before they end. This is especially clear in triangles, and in wedges in particular. With triangles, the breakout is usually imminent but the direction is often not clear. The steeper the slope and the closer together the lines are, the stronger the channel is and the stronger the momentum is. When a channel is steep and tight, it is a special type of channel called a tight channel. When it is horizontal, it is a tight trading range, which is discussed in book 2. When a channel is strong, it is risky to trade the first breakout against the trend, and it is likely that the entire channel will be a spike on a higher time frame chart. So if there is a steep bear channel and most of the pullbacks within the channel have been only a single bar, it is better not to buy one of those breakouts above the prior bar, even if it breaks above the bear trend line. Instead, it is better to wait to see if there is a breakout pullback, which can be a lower low or a higher low. If there is and the reversal up looks strong (for example, maybe there were two or three good-sized bull trend bars within the past several bars), then you can consider buying the breakout pullback. If there is no pullback and the market races upward, then the odds of even higher prices are good and you can wait for any pullback, which should come within five bars or so.

When there is a trend and then it has a pullback, it is common to see a micro trend line in the pullback. For example, in a pullback in a bull trend, if there is a bear micro trend lasting about three to 10 bars, and then there is a break above that bear micro trend line, this theoretically sets up a short on the failed breakout. Since this is occurring during a bull trend and it almost always happens above or near the moving average, you should not be shorting this pattern. You would ﬁnd yourself holding a short at the bottom of a bull ﬂag near a rising moving average in a bull trend, which is a very low-probability trade. As this short will likely fail, you should anticipate this and be ready to buy the failure, getting in exactly where the trapped shorts will get out. Your long will be a breakout pullback buy since the market broke above the bear micro trend line and then pulled back to either a small lower low or a higher low, and then the market resumed in the direction of the breakout, which is also the direction of the major trend of the day.

↳ Adds an explicit invalidation threshold to the false-breakout: price must rise less than 10 percent after the upward breakout and then close below the bottom of the chart pattern (not merely return inside the range)
↳ Busted double bottom: confirmed reversal pattern fails after a short climb (<1 percent) and price closes back through the pattern, confirming as a double top on a close below support (H), triggering a down move

↳ Busted symmetrical triangle: after an upward breakout a throwback takes price below the triangle apex, invalidating the breakout and opening a drop toward support
↳ Busted triple bottom: buy at the breakout (a penny above the highest peak), price deflates back below the pattern bottom, and a stop placed below the bottom of the chart pattern exits the failed trade
↳ Exit rule derived from the busted pattern: once price busts a chart pattern it usually means a strong move down, so sell
↳ After a false upward breakout, price returns inside the pattern (busts) repeatedly; the trader is stopped out on a later bust

Triangle Failures. For the rest of you mere mortals, imagine that you have a buy stop a penny above the top of the ascending triangle shown in Exhibit 19.1. Price breaks out upward at A, and you are overjoyed at getting in on the ground floor of an advance. Then, just three days later, your mood changes when price drops and busts the triangle for the first time. Fortunately, the stock remains above the bottom of the chart pattern where you have a stop loss order. Price climbs above the top of the triangle and you are smiling again. The smile is brief because price drops, busting the pattern for the second time. This time, the stock drops far enough to hit your stop and take you out of the trade for a loss. Almost as soon as the stock cashes you out, it turns, rises, and busts the triangle for the third time. In fact, the busting continues until the stock moves more than 10 percent away from the top of the triangle.

Price closes above the top of the chart pattern. 4. Buy at the open the next day.

↳ False breaks are interpreted as lack-of-momentum clues (not directional signals), occurring at levels of support and resistance that both trader groups identify
↳ The dominant described behavior is the fade: trading against the false break to turn the trap into an opportunity
↳ Introduces the close-based complement: 'trade the break' requires prices to close above resistance or below support, stated as 'the biggest difference' from fade the break
↳ Breakout trigger is a candle CLOSE beyond the established range boundary (close above resistance / below support), not a wick
↳ Entry with the break at the next candle open once momentum is building on that side
↳ Concept text places the stop at the range MIDPOINT, while the author's own execution steps (093/095) specify the 60% mark of the range - an internal inconsistency in the same chapter

↳ Entry requires the breakout candle to close beyond resistance; long entry at the next candle open
↳ No indicators are used for trade-the-break
↳ Short-side mirror of the breakout-with-momentum behavior: breakout candle closes below support; short entry at next candle open
↳ Stop is placed above the support at the 60% mark of the prior range
↳ rally carries the supertrend label
The main reason why false breaks occur is due to the tussle between retail and institutional traders. Both groups of traders easily identify levels of support and resistance, and false breaks are big clues for us retail traders that there is a lack of momentum to push prices further. Remember that false breaks are traps to catch day traders off guard. However, fade the break helps us to turn these traps into opportunities.
17 Proven Currency Trading Strategies - How to Profit in the Forex Market 2013 · s.131 · book_0002::lead_book_0002_1_091
Trade the break is all about momentum. A big clue is seen when prices close above resistance or below support. This clue tells us that momentum is building strongly on one side. When prices close above resistance, that candle is called the breakout candle. A long trade is then taken at the opening price of the next candle. The stop loss is placed below the midpoint of the prior range because we do not expect prices to fall back below that point. When prices close below support, that candle is also called the breakout candle. A short trade is then taken at the opening price of the next candle. The stop loss is placed above the midpoint of the prior range because we do not expect prices to rise above that point.
17 Proven Currency Trading Strategies - How to Profit in the Forex Market 2013 · s.132 · book_0002::lead_book_0002_1_092
We use the AUD/USD on M15 time frame to illustrate long trades. Here are the steps to execute the trade the break strategy for long: 1. Use at least two lows and two highs to identify the support and resistance levels. 2. Identify a candle that closes above the resistance. This is the breakout candle. 3. Enter long at the opening of the next candle. 4. Set the stop loss at the 60% mark of the range (distance between the support and resistance) below the resistance. 5. Set two profit targets for this trade. The targets are set at a risk to reward ratio of 1:1 and 1:2 respectively.
17 Proven Currency Trading Strategies - How to Profit in the Forex Market 2013 · s.132 · book_0002::lead_book_0002_1_093
We use the AUD/USD on M15 time frame for illustrating short trades. Here are the steps to execute the trade the break strategy for short: 1. Use at least two lows and two highs to identify the support and resistance levels. 2. Identify a candle that closes below the support. This is the breakout candle. 3. Enter short at the opening of the next candle. 4. Set the stop loss at the 60% mark of the range (distance between the support and resistance) above the support. 5. We set two profit targets for this trade. The targets are set at a risk to reward ratio of 1:1 and 1:2 respectively.

↳ The first pullback after a strong bull spike is bought by bulls who missed the spike; it is a with-trend continuation buy (high 1) once a true pullback bar (low below the prior bar low) forms.
↳ Aggressive bulls buy above the low of the prior bar, so the pullback may not fall below the prior bar low at all.
↳ When bulls holding profitable longs think the spike is weakening, some sell at the market; others wait for the close and sell if the bar is not another strong bull trend bar.
↳ High 1 / low 1 pullback entries are valid only in a strong bull/bear spike and NOT after a buy/sell climax.
↳ The simple existence of a trend is reason enough to enter at least a small position.
↳ When the reversal occurs within a steep bear channel, wait for a pullback after the reversal up before buying (do not chase the reversal).
↳ Bulls should wait for more strength when the higher low is made of sideways bars with big tails.
↳ When the opening range is a small trading range, most traders prefer to wait for the breakout of the entire opening range.
↳ Pullback entry in an established trend-from-the-open bear trend via a low 2 short and a breakout pullback short
↳ Traders typically wait for the breakout below the first bar of the day (or below the bear flag) before entering the short
↳ Pullback entries in an established bull trend include double bottom bull flag setups and high 2 longs (bar 6 as the high 1)
↳ Buying just above the low of a strong bull trend bar (which a strong bull trend usually does not fall below) is a low-risk, high-reward pullback entry
↳ Multiple pullback entry variants coexist within one established bull trend: a high 2 buy setup after a double bottom, a wedge bull flag, and a breakout pullback buy setup after a bull flag breakout (all with-trend pullback-to-support entries; trend resumes).
↳ A spike-and-channel bull trend often ends on the third push up and is then followed by a correction (channel termination condition).
↳ Requires a strong/established trend: the first two-legged pullback to the moving average in a strong bull trend is a buy ('a great buy').
↳ With-trend entries in a strong trend should be mostly swung, only a small portion taken off as a scalp.
↳ When a spike occurs against a strong trend it often has just one more push and becomes a two-legged bull flag (pullback shape).
↳ If the market stays away from the moving average for 20 bars or more, the trend is very strong and the odds are high that buyers will appear at the moving average (20 gap bar buy setup).
↳ High 2 buy setup: a small second leg down (after a small first leg) is a buy setup in a bull trend, with a high 2 breakout signal bar and the high 1 being the prior bar.
↳ The first breakout of a bull micro channel on a strong bull day is a setup for a buy at one tick above its high.
↳ On a strong trend day, short only after a strong bear leg that broke a trend line; otherwise view all short setups as buy setups and place buy stops where the weak shorts would cover.
↳ Pullback entries are gated by the number of completed countertrend legs (high/low 1, 2, 3, 4 bar-counting) rather than any pullback to support; e.g. a low 2 entry requires two completed legs up before entry.
↳ Channel is expressed as a series of small trading ranges after a spike; in such trending-range regimes take only with-trend pullback entries (two-bar reversal, 20-gap-bar high 2, final-flag reversal).
↳ In an established bear trend/channel, short pullbacks (with-trend) on low 2 triggers and below bear reversal bars
↳ A pullback short can be a dueling-lines setup forming a double top with the earlier pullback and a wedge bear flag

The bulls will be relieved to get out with a smaller loss, and the bears see this as a great opportunity to short above the high of the prior bar in a new bear trend (it might be a bear channel), but if the market falls below the high 2 buy signal bar's low, even the most diehard bulls will give up, and the market will often break out into a bear spike and then at least a measured move down.

When there is a trend and then it has a pullback, it is common to see a micro trend line in the pullback. For example, in a pullback in a bull trend, if there is a bear micro trend lasting about three to 10 bars, and then there is a break above that bear micro trend line, this theoretically sets up a short on the failed breakout. Since this is occurring during a bull trend and it almost always happens above or near the moving average, you should not be shorting this pattern. You would ﬁnd yourself holding a short at the bottom of a bull ﬂag near a rising moving average in a bull trend, which is a very low-probability trade. As this short will likely fail, you should anticipate this and be ready to buy the failure, getting in exactly where the trapped shorts will get out. Your long will be a breakout pullback buy since the market broke above the bear micro trend line and then pulled back to either a small lower low or a higher low, and then the market resumed in the direction of the breakout, which is also the direction of the major trend of the day.

Other bulls who missed the initial buy or did not buy enough during the spike eagerly wait for the first pullback to buy or to add to their positions. They place limit orders at and below the low of the prior bar, hoping for a small dip, so that they can get long. Because of this, the first pullback usually only falls below the low of the prior bar by a few ticks. When the bulls are particularly aggressive, they will buy above the low of the prior bar... Eventually, there will be a true pullback bar, with a low below the low of the prior bar. Once there is, other bulls will place stop orders to buy above its high, because this bar is a high 1 buy setup in a strong bull spike and therefore a high probability buy setup.

With-trend entries in a strong trend should be mostly swung, with only a small potion taken oﬀ as a scalp. If you ﬁnd that you missed a with-trend entry, stop looking for countertrend scalps and start trading only with-trend setups. During a trend day, you must try to catch every with-trend signal, because that is the source of the most consistent money. Since the bar 6 entry bar was a strong bear trend bar, it is a breakout and therefore a spike. Spikes are usually followed by channels with at least two more pushes; but when they occur against a strong trend, they often just have one more push and become a two-legged bull ﬂag. In any case, after a spike down, there was a good chance for at least one more leg down. Bar 7 was an entry bar for a low 2 short into the second leg down, but after a six-bar tight trading range, any breakout in either direction would likely fail after not going very far. Bar 8 was a two-legged pullback and the ﬁrst to the moving average in a strong bull trend, which is a great buy. Whenever the market stays away from the moving average for 20 bars or more (a 20 gap bar buy setup), the trend is very strong and the odds are high that there will be buyers at the moving average. Bar 9 was a reversal at a new swing high, but there were no bear trend bars among the prior seven bars so no short could be taken unless a second entry forms. Bar 13 was a breakout test that extended one tick below the high of the signal bar that generated the strong move up from the bar 8 long.

following a higher high at bar 9, and is part of trending bull swings. It is essentially a double bottom bull ﬂag with bar 8. Bar 14 was a high 2 breakout signal bar, and the high 1 was the prior bar. Bar 15 was a signal bar for a ﬁnal ﬂag short but the market never triggered the entry because it did not trade below the signal bar low. However, as a bear bar, it was a small leg down. The next bar was a bull trend bar and then there was another bear trend bar. This second bear trend bar was a small second leg down and therefore was a high 2 buy setup. Bar 17 was the ﬁrst breakout of a bull micro channel on a strong bull day, and therefore it was a setup for a buy at one tick above its high. The channel had a wedge shape and, although traders would not short here, the theoretical protective buy stop for shorts is one tick above the high of the wedge. Bar 18 broke above a bull trend channel line and gave a low 2 short signal. However, on a strong trend day, smart traders will short only if there is ﬁrst a strong bear leg that broke a trend line. Otherwise, they would view all short setups as buy setups, and place orders to go long exactly where the weak shorts would have to cover (like one tick above the highs of bars 17 and 19). Bar 19 was a one-bar trend line break that failed, and therefore a buy setup. There was a two-bar bull reversal that became the signal for the long.

↳ The pullback ends at the moving average: a two-legged pullback to the moving average, where a two-bar reversal bottom is a buy setup and the trend resumes.
↳ In a steep trend, never buy above a two-bar reversal top; instead view the bull bar as a one-bar bear flag and consider shorting below it (context caveat).
↳ Support line is tested repeatedly to the tick and continues to find buyers
↳ The support line was located one tick below the initial bar 5 entry bar (entry above the two-bar reversal setup at the low of the day)
↳ The market ran the stops below that entry bar by one tick but could not go any further down — interpreted as strong bulls at work
↳ Buyers repeatedly stepped in at support (double bottom pullback longs, higher lows), confirming the bounce
↳ Exhaustion is signaled by an unusually large (climax) trend bar in an extended trend, followed by a spike-and-reverse, not a failed new extreme
↳ The unusually large trend bar forms in a trend that has lasted for 10 or more bars
↳ It often collapses through a trend channel line and acts as a sell climax
↳ The spike down then spike up (breakout above the bull inside bar with a shaved top) is the reversal; it can appear as a two-bar reversal or a single reversal bar on higher time frames
↳ The failed upside breakout is a reversal-bar-confirmed false breakout (bull spike without follow-through), not a range-boundary breach
↳ A two-bar reversal signal followed a strong bull trend bar on a gap down, marking a failed breakout setup and a possible low of the day
↳ There was a four-bar bull spike but no follow-through
↳ The reversal tested the bar 2 start of the spike-and-channel bear trend
↳ A three-bar pattern only forms a valid 15 minute reversal when the third bar closes at the hour boundary (30 minutes after the hour).
↳ Traders should not spend time looking for three-bar reversals because they occur only a couple of times a day.
↳ When a reversal bar almost entirely overlaps the bar before it, it should be considered a two-bar reversal setup.
↳ Shorting below a large bear bar can be risky when the market has been trending up strongly (e.g., nine bars).
↳ A two-bar reversal top is a reliable short only at the end of a buy climax and only when the two-bar reversal is strong
↳ Entry is short below the lower of the two overlapping bars, not below the other
↳ In a strong bull trend, short only below a strong bear bar, never below a strong bull bar
↳ Two-bar reversals are countertrend signals only if there is a reason to expect a reversal
↳ Qualifying condition for the reversion long: a two-bar reversal sell setup just below the moving average with bars that are relatively large and overlap one or more other bars
↳ The reversion is a scalp at the bottom of a small trading range (buy at or below the low of the signal bar), not a swing
↳ The moving average acts as the band; the small correction up to the moving average is the overextension being faded
↳ The setup preceding a major breakout is intentionally weak (small dojis) and traps traders into waiting, so the initial breakout runs
↳ Entering on the low-probability pre-breakout setup or on the higher-probability post-breakout setups are both stated to be mathematically sound
↳ Two-bar reversal (candlestick reversal pattern) is fractal across time frames: the same pattern appears at multiple higher time frames and can collapse into a single bull reversal bar.
↳ Reversal-bar quality is context-dependent: a reversal setup can be an entry bar (e.g., outside up bar after a pause bar following a breakout), and weakness in one bar (tail at top) can be erased by the trend bars that follow.
↳ When the market is trying to go up, it is good to buy above pullbacks (with-trend continuation)
↳ A failed reversal attempt becomes just a pullback from the breakout — the reversal does not reverse the trend
↳ In a bull trend, a single bear reversal bar is not a short setup; wait for a pullback to buy (a two-bar reversal at the moving average is a good setup).
↳ The pullback buy requires the trend to be intact: buying above a bear trend bar after a buy climax/parabolic move is risky because of the risk of a sideways-to-down correction.
↳ Dojis and largely overlapping bars in a strong bull trend rule out the short and favor waiting for the pullback long.
↳ An exact test of an earlier low (prior support level) is a reasonable long setup on a trading range day.
↳ A weak reversal bar is tradable only when there is an additional reason (exact test of a prior low, failed breakout of a flag, or a two-bar reversal buy confirmation).
↳ Context filter: support bounces are favored on trading range days.
↳ Channel is expressed as a series of small trading ranges after a spike; in such trending-range regimes take only with-trend pullback entries (two-bar reversal, 20-gap-bar high 2, final-flag reversal).
↳ Every reversal is a type of two-bar reversal; a classic reversal bar is a two-bar reversal on some smaller time frame, and all climactic reversals, reversal bars, and two-bar reversals are present at all reversals
↳ Reversal bar can be the second bar of a two-bar reversal; when it overlaps more than about 75 percent of the prior bar it should be treated as a two-bar reversal setup rather than a reversal bar (higher odds of success)
↳ Author caveat (page 119, counterevidence): most named candle patterns have no high-probability predictive value most of the time
↳ The band is a trend channel line (micro channel overshoot past a parallel of the bars 1-4 micro trend line, also drawable from the lows) rather than a statistical volatility band
↳ The fade is executed on a two-bar reversal / ii setup at the overshoot, fading a strong bear trend; both bars with bull closes is the desirable ii form
↳ Channel overshoot becomes the first bar of the two-bar reversal; the following bar completes the reversal
The best-known version is a pair of consecutive 5 minute trend bars of approximately the same size but opposite directions. A long setup is a bear trend bar immediately followed by a bull trend bar, and a bear setup is a bull trend bar immediately followed by a bear trend bar. These two bars create a 10 minute reversal bar, but the reversal bar is evident on the 10 minute chart only 50 percent of the time because only half of the 5 minute two-bar reversals will end at the same time as the 10 minute bar.

An unusually large trend bar that forms in a trend that has lasted for 10 or more bars usually means that the market is exhausted and will correct for at least 10 bars, and sometimes it leads to a reversal. In Figure 6.3, bar 3 was a huge trend bar that collapsed below the low of the open and through a trend channel line and was followed by a bull inside bar with a shaved top, meaning that buyers were aggressively buying it right into its close. This is a great setup for a long. The large bear trend bar was acting as a sell climax, and the breakout above the bull inside bar was a bull breakout. This is a spike down and then a spike up, which is a reversal, and if you looked at various higher time frame charts, you could find one or more where this bottom was a perfect two-bar reversal and others where this formed a single reversal bar.

Trading Price Action Trends - Technical Analysis of Price Charts Bar by Bar for the Serious Trader 2011 · s.144 · book_0114::lead_book_0114_2_037
A bear reversal bar in a bull trend is not enough reason to go short and it sometimes becomes a bull flag. In Figure 6.17, the bar after bar 1 was a strong bear reversal bar but it followed five strong bull trend bars. In the absence of no prior strength by the bears, it was not a short setup. Only a second entry could have been considered, which was a short below bar 2. However, bar 2 was a doji and there were four largely overlapping bars in a strong bull trend. Rather than short, it was better to wait for a pullback to buy. The two-bar reversal at the moving average four bars later was a good setup. Although buying above a bear trend bar in a bull spike is often a good trade, buying above the bear trend bar here or above the bull reversal bar that followed it was risky. Bar 1 was a large bull trend bar after several other bull trend bars and it was therefore climactic. There was too much risk of a sideways to down correction after a buy climax. If you look at the highs of the bars up to bar 1, the slope was increasing. This parabolic curvature is also a sign of climactic behavior and that makes the risk of a correction significant. Buying a pullback or looking for a short was a safer approach.

↳ In a strong (trend-from-the-open) bull trend, do not sell the first pullback; the first pullback is almost always followed by a test of the high within a few bars (the trend resumes after the pullback).
↳ The trend can reverse at any time, especially in the first hour, even with strong upward momentum (risk caveat).
↳ After any type of climax, the correction unfolds in two legs and lasts at least 10 bars.
↳ In a trend-from-open day, if the market trends from the first bar or so and the initial spike lasts three or more bars, entering on the first pullback is usually good for at least a scalp (the pullback resolves with trend continuation).
↳ If the opening range of the day is less than 25 percent of the average daily range of recent days, there may be a double bottom on a bull trend day or a double top on a bear trend day (the pullback/consolidation takes a two-legged form); at about 50 percent a breakout is more likely to lead to a trending trading range day.
↳ Trend-from-open days have the smallest pullbacks (a qualifying property of the regime in which the pullback-continuation behavior is asserted).
↳ In a strong trend-from-open day the pullback is usually just a higher-time-frame two-legged correction (e.g., a pullback to the 15-minute moving average) even when it is strong enough to look like a reversal; enter with the trend on pullbacks.
↳ On small-pullback trend days the pullbacks are very small all day; about two-thirds of these days have a larger pullback after 11:00 a.m. PST, often about twice the size of the biggest pullback since the trend began in the first hour.
↳ A late larger pullback heralded by relatively large, strong trend bars in the direction of the trend (climactic exhaustion) signals the end of the move for the time being and the start of a two-legged pullback lasting about 10 bars.
↳ Spike must begin during the first few bars for the day to count as a trend-from-the-open day (regime qualifier)
↳ After the spike the market may soon reverse and break out in the other direction, yielding a spike-and-channel trend, a trending trading range day, or a trading range day
↳ Small pullbacks that never reach the moving average still form high-probability swing setups in a small-pullback bull trend day
↳ All pullbacks in trend-from-the-open days are with-trend entries even when they look weak
↳ 'Any sideways movement was a pause and a type of pullback and was a buy setup'
↳ small pullback day is 'the strongest type of trend day' - pullbacks within a trend are continuation entries
↳ 'the odds are overwhelming that the market will make another high before the pullback retraces very far'
↳ author adds: a strong first trend bar on a gap day predicts follow-through in its direction; when the first two bars are strong, an attempted reversal usually becomes a lower high
↳ author adds: a large gap up with strong selling usually becomes a trend-from-the-open bear trend day; a failed opening reversal results in a lower high or double top
↳ differs from registry: the first bar’s direction on a gap day signals continuation (a trend from the open) away from the fill, with only a brief counter-move expected after a support break, rather than a reversion toward filling the gap (registry gap_reversion direction is toward_fill).
↳ Sell climax is constituted by consecutive large bear trend bars; the sell-off to a new low with no follow-through is attributed to a sell vacuum rather than strong bears
↳ First pullback in a trend-from-open bull trend is a buy setup (with-trend, expect trend resume)
↳ Pullback form specified: gap-up day pullback that tests the low of the open commonly becomes a bull trend day; bar 3 low made a possible double bottom with the bar 1 low
↳ Shorting the top bar is only avoided when there is no sign of a top or buy climax (author caveat on the pullback entry)
↳ Regime qualifier: when the opening range is greater than about 30 percent of the average range of recent days, breakout mode is not good and any bull trend is expected to be weaker
↳ Reversal form specified: the exhaustion originates as a final-flag buy climax — a strong bull trend bar breakout of a largely horizontal bull flag at the end of a protracted bull trend — which triggers a bear spike reversal
↳ Entry triggers: short below the bull trend bar, below the first bar (small bear body), or below the bottom of the final flag
↳ Follow-through specified: entry bar is a large bear spike followed by a tight, very strong bear channel; the day becomes a trend-from-open bear trend day
↳ The first reversal attempt of micro channels is due to profit taking by bulls (mechanism for the flag reversal)

rimary characteristics of trend from the open days: r The low of a bull trend day or the high of a bear trend day is formed within the first few bars of the day. r If the opening range of the day is less than 25 percent of the average daily range of recent days, there may be a double bottom on a bull trend day or a double top on a bear trend day (if the opening range is about 50 percent of the average daily range, a breakout is more likely to lead to a trending trading range day). r The day may begin with a strong spike lasting many bars or it may have a small opening range. r If the market trends from the first bar or so and the initial spike lasts three or more bars, entering on the first pullback is usually good for at least a scalp. r If there is a strong spike on the open that lasts many bars and covers many points, the day will usually become a spike and channel trend day. r A large gap opening often leads to a trend from the open day, and the trend can go in either direction. When there is a large gap up and a trend from the open day forms, the day will be a bull trend day about 60 percent of the time and a bear trend day 40 percent of the time. The opposite is true for gap down openings. The larger the gap, the more likely the day will be a trend day and the more likely the trend will be in the direction of the gap. r Trend from the open days have urgency and conviction from the outset and are usually the strongest trends and have the smallest pullbacks. r Twenty gap bar and moving average gap bar setups come late in the trend.

This type of trend can be so strong that there can be follow-through in the first hour or two of the next day, so traders should be looking to enter with trend on pullbacks after the open of the next day. The pullback often is strong enough to make traders wonder if the market is reversing, but it is usually just a higher time frame, two-legged correction, like a pullback to the 15 minute moving average. However, most traders would find it easier to simply read only one chart when trading and there is always a 5 minute setup at the end of the pullback. As a trend from the open day is evolving, the pullbacks are often very small all day long. When this happens, this is a small pullback trend day. This is the strongest type of trend day and it forms only once or twice a month. About two-thirds of these days have a larger pullback after 11:00 a.m. PST. That pullback is often about twice the size of the biggest pullback since the trend began in the first hour. It is often heralded by a relatively large, strong trend bar or two in the direction of the trend, but representing climactic exhaustion. Take the example of a small pullback bull trend day when the biggest pullback has been nine ticks and the market has been channeling up all day. If sometime between 11:00 a.m. PST and noon the market has two relatively large consecutive bull trend bars breaking out to a new high, the move is more likely an exhaustive buy climax than the start of a new leg. Climaxes are discussed more in the third book, but when a trend has gone on for a long time and then has unusual further strength, it usually signals the end of the move for the time being and the start of a two-legged pullback that will last about 10 bars or so.

When the spike begins during the first few bars, the day is a trend from the open day. When there is a strong trend that might be reversing into a trading range or into an opposite trend, traders will want a strong reversal setup, which is often simply called a reversal. This is because trends are resistant to change and if traders are to bet on a move in the opposite direction, they will want a strong sign that the market is about to reverse. However, if there is a strong trend and then a pullback, traders are so confident that the trend will resume that they will not require a strong reversal setup at the end of the pullback. In fact, the majority of signal bars for trend pullback trades look weak.

↳ The false breakout is a brief countertrend reversal attempt inside an established (bear) trend rather than a range boundary breach, and the post-failure move is with the prior trend.
↳ The failing reversal breakout traps traders into the wrong (long) direction and is usually followed by a breakout in the other direction (with the prior trend).
↳ Less often the reversal breakout succeeds and retraces all or part of the opening bear trend.
↳ Three countertrend lazy pushes form a wedge flag; a third leg failing to surpass the second forms a head and shoulders flag (most head-and-shoulders reversals fail and become continuation patterns).
↳ Multiple pullback entry variants coexist within one established bull trend: a high 2 buy setup after a double bottom, a wedge bull flag, and a breakout pullback buy setup after a bull flag breakout (all with-trend pullback-to-support entries; trend resumes).
↳ A spike-and-channel bull trend often ends on the third push up and is then followed by a correction (channel termination condition).
↳ In an established bear trend/channel, short pullbacks (with-trend) on low 2 triggers and below bear reversal bars
↳ A pullback short can be a dueling-lines setup forming a double top with the earlier pullback and a wedge bear flag
↳ After a failed upside breakout of the day's high, the market once again attempts a breakout of the opposite end of the range (two-sided trading range day) rather than a clean return-inside reversal.
↳ Trading range days often close in the middle of the range.
↳ Measured-move targets are used for exits: initially use the smallest opening-range possibility (bar 2 to bar 3); if the market does not pause there, escalate to the next larger possibilities (bar 3 to bar 4, or bar 3 to bar 6).
↳ Reversals are attributed to computer algorithms based on some measurement; there is almost always some type of measured move in the equation even when not obvious.

↳ The bottoms do not have to be exactly at the same price (micro double bottom tolerance)

↳ Author caveat (page 119, counterevidence): most named candle patterns have no high-probability predictive value most of the time
A micro double bottom is consecutive or nearly consecutive bars with identical or nearly identical lows. When it forms in a bear spike and it is a bear trend bar closing on or near its low and then a bull trend bar opening on or near its low, it is a one-bar bear flag. If the lows are identical, consider selling at one tick below the low. At all other times, it is more likely a reversal pattern, since most small bull reversals come from some type of micro double bottom (discussed in book 3).

this is a shrinking stairs pattern and indicates waning momentum. It often leads to a two-legged reversal and a trend line break. Many three-push reversals qualify as stairs or shrinking stairs trends that failed and reversed. Stairs are often just pullbacks or flags in higher time frame trends, and it is common to see stairs over the final hour or two of the day and then a breakout of the flag on the open of the next day. For example, a broad bull channel today might just be a large bear flag, and the bear trend could break out tomorrow. Alternatively, one stair might suddenly accelerate and break out of the trend channel in the with-trend direction. If it then reverses, this overshoot and reversal will likely result in at least a two-legged move. If it does not, the breakout will probably continue for at least two more legs or at least the approximate height of the channel in an imprecise measured move (the distance beyond the channel should be about the same as the distance within the channel).

We use the EUR/USD on the M30 time frame to illustrate long trades. Here are the steps to execute the fade the break strategy for long: 1. Identify the support level. 2. Identify a candle that has a shadow that goes below the support level. 3. Wait for that candle to close as a bull candle. This is called the false-break candle. 4. Enter at the opening of the next candle. 5. Set a stop loss of 5 pips below the low price of the false break candle. 6. Set two profit targets for this trade. Set the two targets at a risk to reward ratio of 1:1 and 1:2 respectively.

Both groups of traders easily identify levels of support and resistance, and false breaks are big clues for us retail traders that there is a lack of momentum to push prices further. A rally from any three-push pattern usually results in at least two legs up, which ultimately developed here. Bar 2 was a breakout pullback that led to another small rally, but then the market lost momentum. It continued to weakly trend above the moving average until bar 3. At this point, it was clear that something was not right. A trend from the open bull trend is one of the strongest forms of trends but this was clearly not trending strongly. That meant that traders would soon decide that the day was not what they thought and they would exit and wait. They would then be looking for a trading range day and a possible new low for the day. It was possible for the bar 2 low to be followed by a double bottom bull flag, but, in the absence of strong early bulls, bears would aggressively push for a new low of the day and the bar 2 low would likely fail. Bar 4 was a second small push below bar 2 and it was followed by a trend into the close, creating a trend resumption bull day, albeit a weak one, and giving the expected second leg up from the expanding triangle bottom. Bar 4 was an exact breakout test of the trend from the open signal bar high.

If it then reverses, this overshoot and reversal will likely result in at least a two-legged move. If it does not, the breakout will probably continue for at least two more legs or at least the approximate height of the channel in an imprecise measured move (the distance beyond the channel should be about the same as the distance within the channel).
Trading Price Action Trends - Technical Analysis of Price Charts Bar by Bar for the Serious Trader 2011 · s.12 · book_0114::lead_book_0114_4_012

↳ Double Top Knockout (DT-KO): prior extreme is a new two-month calendar high plus another new high no sooner than three trading days later (allows the false double top to form)

The guppy burst seeks to exploit trading proﬁts when the market is quiet. There is a window of around three hours between the close of the U.S. market and the opening of the Asian market. The forex market is relatively quiet during this time and tends to move in a gentle yet predictable manner.

The guppy burst method works with the 5-minute candle (M5).

TürAnlamSayfa
CAVEATThe author warns at the outset that trading is extremely hard and markets are close to efficient, so superior risk-adjusted profits are exceedingly difficult to achieve.xii
SCOPE_LIMITTechnical trading can only work in the minority of moments when markets are less than fully random; most of the time nothing a trader does can produce profit.4
REFUTATIONPsychology, discipline and risk management alone cannot create an edge; they are futile without a positive-expectancy system.4
CAVEATA positive expectancy is only meaningful over a large number of trades; small samples can show results far from the theoretical edge.5
REFUTATIONIntraday closing prices are essentially random samples that differ across data providers, so candlestick patterns built on the close are data-provider artifacts rather than robust signals.12
SCOPE_LIMITMost price patterns are random and carry no predictive information; only a minority of market states contain a real edge.13
REFUTATIONNo indicator or combination of tools produces easy, consistent profits.13
SCOPE_LIMITEquilibrium (non-trending) markets behave like random walks and contain no enduring edge, so the method only applies in disequilibrium states.13
CAVEATTrends also appear in purely random data, so the mere presence of a trend does not prove a tradable imbalance exists.14
CAVEATPivot structure is defined after the fact and has no predictive power at the right edge of the chart.16
REFUTATIONSwing and wave methods explain history well but lack predictive power in real time.18
CAVEATA breakout from a trading range may be nothing more than a random, temporary excursion rather than a signal of real buying pressure.20
REFUTATIONThe common reading that repeated closes on the highs show strength is statistically wrong; it more often signals short-term exhaustion.23
REFUTATIONTrading inside triangle patterns is usually a losing proposition because the internal movement is random.27
FAILURE_EXAMPLEAccumulation areas are hard to trade in practice: buyers of breakouts and stop-outs below the range repeatedly execute at exactly the wrong points.33
CAVEATThe single-candle long-lower-shadow pattern has no standalone predictive power; it only gains meaning from higher-time-frame accumulation context.34
CAVEATWhether a mid-trend range is accumulation or distribution often cannot be determined accurately in real time, only in hindsight.38

FAILURE_EXAMPLEBerkshire lost most of its USAir preferred investment (a $268 million write-down on a $358 million investment), and Buffett used it to warn against the gambler's mistake of doubling down to recover a loss.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEBuffett's stock-funded acquisition of Dexter Shoes gave away 2% of Berkshire for a business subsequently wiped out by low-cost foreign competition, a mistake whose cost grew with Berkshire's later value.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEBuffett stopped buying Wal-Mart because the price rose above his $23 anchor, costing Berkshire shareholders an estimated $10 billion in missed gains — an error of omission caused by price anchoring.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEMunger's refusal to buy more Belrich Oil shares because he would have to sell something else cost him an estimated $200 million compounded, illustrating the enormous cost of errors of omission.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEAll four of Berkshire's investment managers matched the market's 37% decline in 2008, so even a disciplined value process did not protect capital in that year; Buffett admits he did not cover himself with glory.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEBuffett overpaid by buying too many NetJets planes at too high a price and needed a management-led turnaround to fix the mistake.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEBuffett's silver position was mistimed by 13 years, showing that even his high-conviction commodity bets can be badly early.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEClosing out Gen Re's derivatives portfolio cost Berkshire $400 million even though the positions were marked to market and audited, showing that mark-to-market accounting on complex instruments can hide real losses.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEThe market-timing advice of two respected elders (Graham and Buffett's father) that it was a bad time to enter the securities business was wrong: waiting would have left Buffett with his original $10,000 instead of the fortune he built.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEBuffett admits his famous October 2008 'Buy American. I Am.' call was premature — markets fell much further after it — even though the long-run direction proved right.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEBerkshire itself issued stock at an overpriced level in the mid-1990s, and even Buffett and Munger said on the prospectus that they would not buy at that price — an admission of a value-destructive capital move by the most celebrated allocator.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEBerkshire lost a few hundred million dollars on Irish banks, an investment Buffett himself called his big idea, and which turned out far worse than Munger's BYD.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEMunger's early venture capital investment failed badly — the key inventor left and the product was obsolesced — souring him on technology ventures for decades.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEA tiny GEICO commercial insurance book ($72,000 of premium) produced a $94 million loss, showing that small positions in insurance can generate enormous tail losses.0
FAILURE_EXAMPLEMutual of Omaha destroyed half its net worth in a short time by entering property/casualty reinsurance, a cautionary tale that venturing into an unfamiliar line can undo decades of accumulation.0
CAVEATThe margin of safety must be large because the method rests on estimates that can be wrong and on luck that can be worse than average.0
CAVEATLeverage can destroy even sound positions because you may not survive the drawdown before the trade works out.0
CAVEATIf you cannot estimate a business's future cash flows with reasonable accuracy, the method instructs you not to invest in it at all.0
CAVEATRelying on historical statistics and formulas risks betting on a great past record that no longer holds — a horse ready for the glue factory.0
CAVEATEven a wonderful business is a bad investment at too high a price, and Buffett warned that the overpayment risk was elevated when he said this.0
CAVEATFollowing more than about 40 companies destroys an investor's edge; even 8-10 good ideas in a lifetime is enough, so breadth of coverage is itself a limit on performance.0
CAVEATIf a company's accounting is confusing, the method says avoid it, because the confusion may be deliberate and a signal of management character.0
CAVEATDiscounted-cash-flow valuation breaks down when the assumed growth rate exceeds the discount rate, producing an infinite value, so high-growth projections must be forced down to realistic numbers.0
CAVEATIn stress, exposures that seemed independent correlate and become one unrecognized concentration of risk, so diversification across nominally different assets is not real protection.0
CAVEATIn insurance, a few large mistakes can undo years of wealth accumulation, so the discipline must be to decline business rather than chase volume.0
CAVEATReasonable forward stock returns are only 6-7% a year, and expecting 15% is unrealistic.0
CAVEATEven passive index investing can fail badly when prices get too high, as Japan's negative 13-year Nikkei returns show, and standard models failed to predict it.0
CAVEATGold only pays off in catastrophic scenarios, so it is a bet on disaster rather than a general inflation hedge.0
CAVEATBusinesses heavy in receivables and inventory perform badly in inflation, so the inflation-hedge method only works for low-capital businesses with pricing power.0
CAVEATEven sophisticated bank risk models and committees failed to see the 2008 crisis coming; formal risk-management structures can create false comfort.0
CAVEATEven the most successful investors admit they cannot predict the macro environment and would never have forecast five years of zero rates.0
CAVEATThere is no mechanical formula for intrinsic value that works across businesses; Munger puts almost all businesses in a 'too hard' pile, so the method is narrow and hands-on rather than systematic.0
CAVEATThe edge only exists when picking a few spots; trying to evaluate everything eliminates the advantage.0
SCOPE_LIMITThe book explicitly warns readers to model Buffett and Munger's advice rather than copy their behavior, because Berkshire's scale, bespoke deals and whole-company purchases cannot be replicated by most investors.0
SCOPE_LIMITThe insurance-float leverage that drives much of Berkshire's outperformance is unavailable to ordinary investors.0
SCOPE_LIMITBuffett's universe is restricted to large companies, so bargains are scarce for him; small investors are not so restricted and can consider thousands of small companies, meaning his sale decisions do not transfer to them.0
SCOPE_LIMITBerkshire's size forces it to consider only companies with roughly $50 billion market caps, and its future returns will be decent but far below its past.0
SCOPE_LIMITParts of Berkshire's approach — its float, bespoke deals and whole-company purchases — cannot be copied by the average investor.0
SCOPE_LIMITBerkshire's compounding rate will certainly decline from its past levels because of its size.0
SCOPE_LIMITEven skilled investors face a worse environment over the next 50 years than the last 50.0
SCOPE_LIMITThe Berkshire method deliberately excludes technology because winners there are too hard to pick, trading away big payoffs for certainty.0
SCOPE_LIMITAt Berkshire's scale, capital far exceeds the supply of good ideas, so the binding constraint becomes finding something worth buying.0
SCOPE_LIMITBerkshire's rate of gain will inevitably slow, and Munger treats this as unavoidable rather than fixable.0
REFUTATIONCycle-guessing and dancing in and out of positions based on forecasts is refuted as a workable approach; doing so would have wrecked Berkshire's results.0
REFUTATIONStudying the past alone cannot make you rich — the refutation of backtesting and past-performance extrapolation as a source of edge.0
REFUTATIONAttributing future junk-bond performance to the asset class's past record is refuted as a false-causality argument.0
REFUTATIONDiversification is refuted — it is characterized as a confession of ignorance rather than a virtue.0
REFUTATIONThe academic doctrine that diversification is the key is inverted; concentration (non-diversification) is argued to be the key.0
REFUTATIONVolatility and beta are refuted as measures of risk.0
REFUTATIONEfficient market theory is refuted as a grand structure built on a false premise, despite being Nobel Prize material.0
REFUTATIONFinancial projections are refuted as doing more harm than good because they are prepared by people who want a particular outcome.0
REFUTATIONComputer-generated precision is refuted; outputs precise to three decimal places are a sign the analysis is too complicated.0
REFUTATIONThe worst mistakes come from the prettiest charts; graph/technical-based analysis is refuted in favor of common sense.0
REFUTATIONInvesting in fast-growing industries is refuted as a route to riches — AT&T, airlines and autos grew hugely while destroying investor value.0
REFUTATIONEBITDA is refuted as an earnings measure because it ignores real costs like depreciation and taxes.0
REFUTATIONThe common belief that stock buybacks add value is refuted — most buybacks are herd behavior done at high prices and do not add value.0
REFUTATIONBuying IPOs is refuted — insiders choose the timing to sell, so an IPO is unlikely to be the cheapest thing to buy.0
REFUTATIONLeverage is refuted as the consistent cause of financial ruin throughout history, wiping out even high-IQ people.0
REFUTATIONA single valuation ratio like P/E is refuted as a working decision rule — it cannot be that easy.0
REFUTATIONCasino-like day trading is refuted as asinine.0
REFUTATIONThe popular idea that real estate makes people rich is refuted — the big money lost in real estate is forgotten.0
REFUTATIONMuch of what is taught in corporate finance classes is dismissed as twaddle.0
REFUTATIONValue-at-risk is dismissed as one of the dumbest ideas ever put forward because its math does not apply to human behavior in stress.0
CONTRADICTIONThe book first presents Ben Graham's framework in which 'diversified portfolios of such stocks have provided superior returns with below-average risk,' and later has Buffett and Munger reject diversification as 'a protection against ignorance' and assert 'Non-diversification is the key' — two incompatible doctrines on the same question within one book.0
CONTRADICTIONBuffett repeatedly states that the overall market level has no impact on their purchase decisions, yet the same book documents Berkshire repeatedly changing its overall stock/bond/cash exposure in response to market valuations.0
CONTRADICTIONIn the 1995 notes Buffett says a one-newspaper-town newspaper would be the single business he would own; in the 2009 notes he says most newspaper companies today are not a buy at any price — incompatible recommendations on the same asset class within the same book.0

REFUTATIONThe author refutes the possibility of short-term market forecasting: no one can predict the course of the market over the next month or year, regardless of method.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes technical analysis: across all studied forms, no technical strategy has consistently outperformed a buy-and-hold (placebo) strategy after accounting for costs.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes the Dow theory: its buy/sell signals carry no predictive significance, and a Dow follower actually comes out behind buy-and-hold after extra brokerage costs.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes filter/stop-loss-style trading systems: after transactions costs, filter rules cannot consistently beat simply buying and holding.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes the relative-strength system as a consistent edge: it outperforms buy-and-hold only in some periods, and after taxes and costs it is not useful.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes price-volume systems: their signals contain no information useful for prediction, and the forced in-and-out trading makes costs exceed buy-and-hold.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes chart-pattern signals: in a computer scan of 32 chart patterns on 548 NYSE stocks, there was no relationship between technical signals and subsequent performance after costs.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes market timing as a reliable skill, citing Bernard Baruch's maxim that market timing can only be accomplished by liars.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes smart beta's claim of excess returns: multifactor risk models show smart beta portfolios produce no risk-adjusted alpha.1
REFUTATIONThe author reports that beta as a risk measure fails empirically: Fama-French found a flat beta-return relationship, so beta is not a useful single risk/return predictor.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes fundamental analysis: academically it is judged no better than technical analysis at capturing above-average returns.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes analyst earnings forecasting: careful analyst estimates do little better than naive extrapolation, and five-year analyst forecasts were worse than naive models.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes fund-chasing: past fund performance does not persist, and top performers of one period frequently become the worst in the next.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes IPO investing: IPOs have historically been a bad deal, underperforming the market by about 4 percentage points per year five years out.1
REFUTATIONThe author refutes the possibility of smooth consistent double-digit returns (as in the Madoff scheme), arguing such claims are a fraud giveaway.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEHedge funds failed as the arbitrage mechanism: during 1998-2000 they were net buyers of Internet stocks, inflating the bubble rather than correcting mispricing.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLELTCM, a Nobel-laureate-designed hedge fund, failed because its hedged positions moved against it and it ran out of capital.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEShorting overvalued stocks failed: traders who shorted Internet favorites in 1999 lost their shirts because prices kept rising for years before the bubble burst.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEDay trading failed even in a bull market: most Internet traders lost money, performed worse the more they traded, and had an average survival of about six months.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLERAFI's fundamental-indexing excess returns are attributed to greater risk assumption (e.g., 15% of portfolio in Citigroup and Bank of America in 2009), not to exploiting mispricing.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEStatistical analysis of the RAFI PRF returns via the Fama-French three-factor model estimates RAFI's alpha at zero, so no genuine excess performance exists.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEValue funds and value ETFs failed to deliver above-average returns in the 2004-2013 period, contradicting the value premium claim.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEThe top 20 funds of the 1990s collapsed in the 2000s: they had loaded up on New Economy stocks, rode the bubble up, and collapsed when it burst.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEThe Mates Fund, ranked #1 in 1968, lost 93 percent of its value by 1974, exemplifying that top performance does not persist.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEThe Dogs of the Dow strategy consistently underperformed the market after becoming popular, showing popular strategies self-destruct.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEThe January effect is not dependable each year: small-cap trading costs exceed the benefit, and in some years the effect is a mirage.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEMomentum-strategy funds produced subpar results in practice, failing to deliver the academic momentum premium with real money.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLELow-volatility ETFs (SPLV, USMV, LGLV) failed to exceed their cap-weighted benchmarks through Q1 2014.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEThe AQR momentum ETF (AMOMX) failed to produce excess returns over its benchmarks through the first half of 2014.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEThe Beardstown Ladies' claimed 23.9% annual returns were fabricated (dues counted as profits); their true return was 9.1%, below the market.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEThe famous Elliott-wave guru Robert Prechter, after predicting the Dow would fall below 400, missed the entire 1990s bull market.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEElaine Garzarelli, famous for calling the 1987 crash, then stayed bearish and missed the market bounce-back, disappointing investors who followed her.1
FAILURE_EXAMPLEWall Street analysts' strong-buy recommendations underperformed the market by 3% per month while sell recommendations outperformed by 3.8%, showing analyst ratings fail.1
CAVEATThe author qualifies the random-walk model: it does not strictly hold and some short-term momentum / long-term mean reversion patterns appear to exist.1
CAVEATMomentum should not be relied on for a surefire edge: prices sometimes overreact and reversals can be sudden, so short-term momentum is not dependable.1
CAVEATContrarian buying of long-term losers produced statistically strong return reversals but no higher-than-average returns, so the pattern is not exploitable.1
CAVEATThe small-firm effect is not dependable or certain to persist; buying small-cap portfolios is not a surefire path to abnormal returns.1
CAVEATPart of the small-firm effect may be an artifact of survivorship bias because only surviving small firms appear in the data.1
CAVEATLow P/E and low P/BV can reflect priced-in risk (e.g., financial distress), so value metrics do not automatically indicate underpricing.1
CAVEATIndexing does not eliminate market risk: if the market falls, the index portfolio falls with it.1
CAVEATIndexing/diversification by definition also rules out extraordinary gains, not only extraordinary losses.1
CAVEATDollar-cost averaging is not optimal in a steadily rising market, where a lump-sum investment up front would do better.1
CAVEATDollar-cost averaging does not eliminate equity risk and cannot protect a portfolio from severe bear markets like 2008.1
CAVEATDollar-cost averaging is not appropriate for investing lump sums such as bequests because of the long-term uptrend in stock prices.1
CAVEATStocks remain risky even over long holding periods: final-value variability increases with holding length and some decades produced near-zero stock returns.1
CAVEATAcademic return-pattern results (e.g., value effect) may be time-dependent and may not be reproducible with real money.1
CAVEATReal-money portfolios generally do not achieve the effectiveness shown in academic simulations, a general caveat on smart beta.1
CAVEATNo strategy works regardless of valuations: strategy effectiveness depends on the market valuations at implementation time.1
CAVEATThe firm-foundation theory's intrinsic value rests on uncertain forecasts of growth extent and duration, making the foundation less dependable than claimed.1
CAVEATThe author argues it is intrinsically impossible to calculate the intrinsic value of a share; there is fundamental indeterminateness in common-share valuation.1
CAVEATThe author qualifies EMH: since future cash flows and risk premiums are uncertain, prices are likely to be wrong all the time, and one can never be sure if they are too high or too low.1
CAVEATArbitrage can fail to correct mispricing because the market can remain irrational longer than the arbitrageur can remain solvent.1
CAVEATArbitrage is constrained when stocks cannot be borrowed for short sales, preventing correction of the most glaring mispricings.1
SCOPE_LIMITThe book's advice is explicitly scoped to long-term investors, not speculators seeking short-term gains or overnight riches.1
SCOPE_LIMITThe author's return-projection methodology is limited to long-run ranges; short-term movements are explicitly unpredictable.1
SCOPE_LIMITThe stocks-beat-bonds claim is scoped to holding periods of 25+ years with dividend reinvestment; shorter horizons do not carry the same assurance.1
SCOPE_LIMITInternational diversification's risk reduction fails in crises: in 2007-09 correlations spiked and all markets fell together, leaving no place to hide.1
SCOPE_LIMITDiversification benefits have eroded: globalization raised correlations between US and foreign markets and between stocks and commodities.1
SCOPE_LIMITMPT's total-risk-elimination is a theoretical ideal; in practice company fortunes move in tandem, so total risk elimination cannot be achieved.1
SCOPE_LIMITEmerging markets may be less efficient but are costly to access and trade (higher expenses, lower liquidity), limiting exploitable inefficiency.1
SCOPE_LIMITTIPS are scoped to tax-advantaged retirement accounts because their inflation adjustments create immediate tax liabilities.1
SCOPE_LIMITJunk-bond investing is scoped to risk-tolerant, diversified investors; it is unsuitable for income-dependent investors and insomniacs.1
CONTRADICTIONThe book defines short-run stock price changes as unpredictable (random walk), yet later reports that the random-walk model does not strictly hold and short-term momentum exists.1
CONTRADICTIONThe book says no one can predict the market over the next month or year, but later endorses buying after sharp market declines because 'what goes down has come back up' for the market as a whole.1
CONTRADICTIONThe behavioral-finance chapter argues markets are not efficient and 'there is no such thing as a random walk,' which contradicts the book's core efficient-market conclusion.1

REFUTATIONThe book refutes the claim that a trained eye can evaluate hitters by watching: the difference between a good and average hitter is invisible to observation.0

REFUTATIONJames refutes the common reading of statistics as pure individual accomplishments, arguing every statistic is the product of the player plus his circumstances.0

CONTRADICTIONThe A's ran a system whose entire premise was that plate discipline (walks) could be taught to minor leaguers, yet Beane concluded discipline cannot be taught after seeing his trained big league hitters be the least disciplined.0
CONTRADICTIONThe book contrasts Beane's stated belief (the game is a predictable social science, so stay calm) with his actual behavior (intense rage, emotional reactions, subjective judgments), an internal contradiction between his method and his conduct.0
CONTRADICTIONThe book presents two competing characterizations of which pitch count matters most—first-pitch strikes versus the 1-2 vs 2-1 third-pitch state—with Paul himself correcting the popular emphasis, an internal tension about which count is the decisive variable.0
